author: Tsuchiya
name_in_asr: Darel (Faxian's 陀歷); Rajikot; Pouguch 'university' site
asr_identification: Pouguch 'university' site, 15.3 km above the mouth of the Darel valley, as the shrine of the wooden Maitreya; Rajikot hill fort as the seat of the ruler; Darel valley, Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan
evidence: Field work 1998–2000 (from the valley mouth up to Horone) and 2003–06 (the heads of the Singal and Darel valleys); no excavation. Two sites: Rajikot, a fortress city on a massive hill with stone walls and a siphoned water supply from the Kotogah river, to which legend attaches a powerful ruler who could have conceived a temple with a colossal image; and Pouguch 'university', whose legends (a place of worship and learning, pilgrims from all quarters, a wooden Buddha) she matches with Faxian. The defences of the valley (the Darband gate of pine 1 km S of Matic, a wall on the left bank, a signal system from the Batakhun pass) lie at its head, none at the mouth, so Pouguch, 15.3 km from the Indus, was in the safest part. Conifer forests of the Khanbari and neighbouring valleys (still Darel's timber trade) explain why this colossal image alone was of wood.
quote: Our field research covered two prominent sites: Rajikot … a fortress city on a massive hill, and Pouguch ‘university’ site, a religious establishment where Fa Hsein could have made his pilgrimage … Therefore Pouguch, located only 15.3 kilometers to the mouth of the valley where Fa Hsien could have visited to worship the colossal Maitreya Buddha, was at the safest place in the Darel Valley.
note: Agrees with the study (Darel, medium). The English paper repeats her Pouguch proposal (Tsuchiya 2010) and adds Rajikot as the possible seat of the ruler, the defensive argument (gate and signal system at the head of the valley) and the timber argument for the wooden image; all from survey and local legend, no excavation, image, inscription or datable find. Faxian-centred; Xuanzang is not mentioned. No change to 03.01.16.

author: Tsuchiya
asr_identification: Faxian's route from the Pamirs to Darel: Khora Bhort pass – Karambar – Ishkoman – Singal – Yajei pass – Atth in the upper Darel valley
evidence: Surveys 2003–06 of the passes between the Singal valley and Darel: the Yajei pass, open all year and used for cattle, is the common route; the Batakhun pass is steep and dangerous; the Gilgit–Kargah–Khanbari route to Darel is twice as long as Singal village–Pouguch.
quote: On the other hand, the Yajei Pass, the pass which never had been highlighted historically, has been confirmed to be the common route used by people and livestock. Now we are able to propose that Fa Hsien could have traveled from Pamir to Darel by way of the Yajei Pass.
note: Faxian's route, not the location of a Xiyu ji place: Xuanzang reached Darel from Udyāna up the Indus. Context only (see lit_batch6 tsuchiya2010:3).

author: Imtiaz and Zahra
evidence: Survey of unreported heritage sites in Kallar Kahar tehsil, Chakwal district: one mound (Pind, 3 km NE of Bhoun, red and orange ware, dated 6th–7th c. CE), Hindu temples, a samadhi, havelis, a baoli, a railway station. Nothing on Ketas, on Buddhist remains or on Xuanzang.
note: Low relevance: no Siṃhapura site is discussed; the Bhoun mound (6th–7th c.) is not linked to anything in the Xiyu ji. Published in Ancient Punjab 5 (2017), pp. 25–; literature.tsv also gives vol. 4.

author: Denisenko, Filatov and Lyamina
evidence: Review of over 60 Kushan-period (1st–early 4th c.) settlement sites in the Kashmir valley, only three excavated (Harwan, Semthan, Kanispur); Kalhaṇa's Huṣkapura, Juṣkapura, Kaniṣkapura with Ushkur and Kanispur (Stein); routes out of the valley. Xuanzang is not mentioned.
note: Background to Kashmir, earlier than Xuanzang; no Xiyu ji place discussed. Citation correction: authors V. L. Denisenko, E. A. Filatov, V. A. Lyamina (literature.tsv has 'V. L. De…'); Russian title 'Поселенческие комплексы кушан в долине Кашмира'.

author: Huang
asr_identification: Vaikuṇṭha Perumāḷ (Tiru Parameswara Vinnagaram) temple, Kāñcīpuram
evidence: Art-historical identification of an East-Asian monk figure on the porch reliefs of the Vaikuṇṭha Perumāḷ temple as Xuanzang, and another figure as Wang Xuance; assumes that Xuanzang stayed at Kāñcī.
note: Does not discuss the location of Kāñcīpura (10.16, secure, high), which it assumes; the identification of the figure is iconographic speculation and not evidence for the place.

author: Chadhar
asr_identification: Eran on the Bina, Sagar district, Madhya Pradesh: occupied to the Huṇa period, then silent until the 9th c.
evidence: Summary of the Sagar University excavations (1960–65, 1986–88, 1998): a burnt layer about one foot thick, which he ties to Mihirakula's attack c. 510 (Goparāja inscription of 510); after the Gupta–Huṇa period no literature, inscription or coin names Airikiṇa, and the settlement history resumes only in the 9th c. under the Gurjara-Pratihāras, after which Eran was in Jejākabhukti (Candella, Paramāra 10th–12th c.). Temples of the Gupta period and the Toramāṇa boar.
quote: Evidence of burning of the entire city has been found from this stratigraphic layer of the Excavation. … We do not hear any more of Airikina neither in later literature nor in inscriptions and coins. After the Guptas, the history of the Eran village settlement can be dated to the Ninth century C.E. … After the Ninth century, the region of Eran was included under the ‘Jejakbhukti’ region.
note: Bears on Eran as the capital of 擲枳陀 (the gazetteers' choice on distance; the study leaves the capital open, Khajuraho or Eran). If the summary is right, the excavated sequence has a gap from the early 6th to the 9th c., i.e. no evidence of a 7th-c. town, which weighs against Eran; but this is a heritage overview, not the excavation report, and 'no evidence' from a limited excavation is not proof of absence. Not mentioned: Xuanzang.

author: Suvrathan
evidence: Banavasi–Gudnapur Regional Survey 2009–12: full-coverage survey of 25 km² round Banavasi, over 350 sites recorded, among them the remains of several possible stūpas. A two-line eroded Brāhmī inscription (de va sa tha te… / tu…, 'of Deva-'), on an outcrop in the Varadā bed over 1 km NE of Banavasi, palaeographically 1st c. BC–early centuries AD; perhaps at a ford; nearness to water may suggest Buddhism. Recalls the 3rd-c. Nāgaśrī inscription recording a tank, vihāra and nāga; Banavasi the Kadamba capital (4th–6th c.) and an administrative centre to the 14th/15th c.
quote: Banavasi rose to prominence as the capital of the regional kingdom of the Kadamba dynasty (4th-6th centuries AD) and continued to maintain its importance as an administrative and regional economic center … While the remains of several possible stupas were identified on survey
note: Background for the Banavasi alternative (11.02, open: Annagundi or Banavasi): survey reports possible stūpas round Banavasi and continuity as a regional centre after the Kadamba period; all early or undated, nothing 7th-c. and nothing naming Koṅkaṇapura; Xuanzang is not mentioned. No change; the fuller report is Suvrathan 2014 (wanted).

author: Deeg
evidence: Research history: how 19th–20th c. scholarship (Rémusat, Wilson, Laidlay, Cunningham, Beal, Legge) treated Faxian's record as secondary to Xuanzang's; Cunningham used Faxian only to correct Xuanzang where it suited his identifications.
note: No identification of a place; historiography only.
